content: 1. Within the education sector, a structured five-step process is outlined for implementing the global standards for Health-Promoting Schools (HPS). This process includes reviewing current activities and practices (Step 3) and developing a comprehensive implementation plan (Step 4), supported by strategies grouped into 13 key areas. 2. Countries may have varying levels of experience with HPS approaches, ranging from no experience to extensive implementation. For example, some countries lack a national school health policy, while others have policies that are outdated or recently updated. The quality of implementation often varies across districts and schools. 3. A 1–2-year implementation plan should align with the strategic and operational planning cycles of the education sector. Districts and schools should be sensitized to the new policy, and expressions of interest should be encouraged, regardless of prior experience with HPS. 4. Early adopters of HPS should receive capacity development support, including training, operational manuals, and tools. Lessons learned from these early implementations should inform broader rollouts. 5. Intersectoral government and multi-stakeholder coordination should be reinforced to ensure effective implementation. Updated policies should be disseminated, and districts and schools should be supported with capacity-building resources. 6. Iterative implementation cycles should be repeated, with rapid gap analyses conducted to identify areas for improvement. If necessary, national standards for HPS should be developed or updated, with strengthened accountability through better reporting on indicators and targets. 7. Investments in school infrastructure, such as facilities and spaces, should support safe, healthy physical and social-emotional environments. Comprehensive school health services should be accessible to all students. 8. Curricula and associated resources should be developed and implemented to promote health and well-being across all subject areas. This includes tools such as assessment instruments, sample lesson plans, and audiovisual materials. 9. Teacher training and professional learning opportunities should be accessible, with initial training programs and in-service learning aligned with HPS curricula and standards. Continuous professional development and certification opportunities should also be provided. 10. Students, parents, caregivers, and the local community should be actively involved in HPS initiatives. Partnerships between schools and communities should be strengthened to foster collaboration. 11. School leadership and governance practices should be enhanced to support sustainable HPS systems. This includes defining leadership models that involve students, community members, and government representatives at various levels. 12. Resources should be allocated effectively to support all components of sustainable HPS systems. This includes reviewing current resource allocations and developing flexible funding models that address local needs and priorities. 13. Evidence-informed practices should guide the planning and design of HPS goals, targets, and activities. Monitoring and evaluation systems should track progress and inform future implementation efforts. 14. Partnerships and sustained collaborations should be developed between national, subnational, and local government departments, as well as between schools and local organizations or businesses, to support HPS systems. 15. Each of the 13 implementation areas is defined and described in detail, with examples from literature and case studies illustrating barriers and enablers for implementation. These areas align with the global standards for HPS and are mapped to specific levels of responsibility (national, subnational, local, or school). 16. Intersectoral coordination involves establishing structures, roles, and responsibilities for HPS coordination groups. This includes identifying key stakeholders across relevant sectors and levels of government, forming multi-stakeholder committees, and developing operational plans for collaboration. 17. National policies or strategies for HPS should include a rationale for coordination and approaches for identifying stakeholders. These policies should reflect the country’s governance structure and organizational frameworks for education and health services. 18. Lessons from evidence highlight the importance of recognizing health as integral to education. Embedding HPS in education policy is more likely when education and health sectors share the view that health is foundational to learning and academic outcomes. 19. Shared leadership between education and health ministries ensures the sustainability of HPS initiatives. Collaborative structures and international expertise in HPS further support policy development and implementation. 20. Policies should explicitly address health and well-being priorities that schools can influence, such as comprehensive sexuality education, violence prevention, menstrual health, life skills, nutrition, and risk factor prevention for noncommunicable diseases. 21. School leaders must be involved in HPS planning to ensure local needs and contexts are addressed. This includes identifying specific health needs of students and available resources to meet those needs. 22. Schools should have ownership of HPS initiatives, with flexibility in development and implementation. Organizational structures that support HPS within schools enhance adoption and collective efficacy, ensuring sustained implementation. 23. Resource allocation for HPS should involve reviewing current allocations and aligning budgets with HPS goals and targets. Flexible funding mechanisms, such as grants, should be available to schools based on their specific needs and contexts. 24. Professional learning opportunities for teachers should be supported through models that allow for flexible use of time and resources. These models should be adaptable to the structure of the teaching workforce in different countries. 25. Evidence-based methods for resource allocation should guide decision-making processes, ensuring that resources are distributed equitably and effectively to support HPS initiatives.
